version.changelog:
- Clarified installation instructions for immediate activation after install.
- Updated onboarding flow details to specify auto-registration with agent name and description.
- Simplified API key configuration steps in command documentation.
- Minor text tweaks for accuracy and readability.

llm.summary: The skill's instructions are largely consistent with a security plugin, but it auto-registers with an external 'Core' service, creates and stores API keys on disk, and will send content to a remote service without fully describing what is transmitted or retained — these behaviors deserve caution before installing.

dimensions.detail: The name and description claim a runtime security plugin and the runtime instructions show installation via the OpenClaw plugin system and delegation of detection to an external 'Core' service — this is coherent for a security plugin. Minor inconsistencies: registry metadata lists Source: unknown while SKILL.md includes a GitHub URL; install/update command formats differ slightly (scoped vs unscoped).
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: The SKILL.md instructs the agent/user to install the plugin and to 'test' by reading a file under ~/.openclaw/extensions/moltguard/ (that path is reasonable). However it also states that 'All security detection is performed by Core' and describes automatic registration that sends agent name/description to Core. The doc does not enumerate what agent data (prompts, file contents, system metadata) is sent to Core or retained, and it includes commands like /og_status that explicitly show your API key — a potential credential-exposure vector. The instructions therefore permit uploading potentially sensitive content to an external service without clear disclosure.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: There is no formal install spec in the skill bundle; instead the SKILL.md directs using the OpenClaw plugin installer (openclaw plugins install @openguardrails/moltguard). This is a standard, lower-risk pattern if the package source is trusted, but the registry metadata marked source unknown while the README references a GitHub repo — you should verify the package origin (registry entry and repository) before running the installer.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill doesn't request environment variables up front, which is reasonable, but the onboarding flow describes auto-creating an API key and saving credentials to ~/.openclaw/credentials/moltguard/. The ability to generate and store API credentials (and commands that display them) is proportionate to a service-backed plugin but also raises privacy/credential-exposure concerns. There is no clear statement about what data is sent to Core, how long it's stored, or retention/ownership policies.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: always:false (no forced inclusion) and the skill is user-invocable/autonomous invocation allowed — normal for plugins. The onboarding flow describes the plugin auto-registering and writing credentials under the user's home directory; this is plausible for a plugin but is an environment modification the user should expect and understand before consenting.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance: Before installing: 1) Verify the package origin — confirm the plugin published to your OpenClaw registry matches the GitHub repo linked in SKILL.md and look at the repo code if possible. 2) Understand data flows — the plugin sends data to an external 'Core' service for analysis; ask what types of content (prompts, file contents, metadata) are transmitted and how long it is retained. 3) Be cautious about credential exposure — the plugin will auto-generate and store an API key at ~/.openclaw/credentials/moltguard/ and provides a command that displays that key; avoid pasting that key into other places or exposing logs. 4) Test in an isolated agent first (non-production) to see exactly what network calls occur. 5) If you cannot confirm the source or data-handling policies, do not install or claim agents that share quota across machines. If you proceed, keep the uninstall commands on hand and review created files under ~/.openclaw after installation.
